newsitem.title: USA: U.S. manufacturers to hold jobs steady - survey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. manufacturers to hold jobs steady - survey.

text.p: Most manufacturers plan to hold employment steady this year while about a third plan to add workers in 1997, a survey said Monday.
The survey by the National Association of Manufacturers also found that many manufacturing executives think the Federal Reserve should cut interest rates, not raise them.

The executives surveyed were convinced that new workers need more education and training. A full 64 percent said a significant number of entry level workers lacked the skills required to increase the company's productivity and growth.
"We can't get the skilled workers we need," association President Jerry Jasinowski said at a news conference.

Of the roughly 400 executives who responded to the survey last month, 55 percent said they would hold employment at or near current levels this year while 33 percent said they would increase full-time permanent jobs.
A full 58 percent said the Federal Reserve should hold interest rates steady but 25 percent called for a quarter-point cut in short-term rates and 16 percent called for a half-point reduction.

"The Fed ought to continue on its very sensible policy of holding its action until it has further evidence of inflation increases," Jasinowski said. The group has pushed to help keep interest rates steady for several months, he added.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said recently that the central bank was ready to raise rates, if needed, in a bid to ward off inflation.
Jasinowki said the lack of skilled entry-level workers was not leading to higher wages in manufacturing because productivity has continued to rise.

In terms of wages, 28 percent of the respondents said they plan to raise wages 2.6 percent to 3 percent in 1997, 14 percent plan 2 percent to 2.5 percent increases and 6 percent plan to raise wages less than 2 percent.
Other respondents plan increases of between 3 percent and 4 percent.
On inventories, 65 percent plan to hold inventories at current levels and 24 percent expect to lower them gradually.
Nearly half plan to boost capital spending less than 5 percent but others planned higher increases.
